content: 1. Severe persistent diarrhea in infants or children is defined as diarrhea lasting 14 days or more, accompanied by signs of dehydration. These cases require hospital treatment. 2. Assess the child for dehydration and provide fluids according to Treatment Plan B or C, as appropriate. 3. For home treatment of diarrhea, counsel the caregiver on four key rules: provide extra fluids, administer zinc supplements, continue feeding, and recognize when to return to the clinic. 4. Encourage breastfeeding frequently and for longer durations. If the child is exclusively breastfed, provide oral rehydration solution (ORS) or clean water in addition to breast milk. 5. For non-exclusively breastfed children, offer ORS, food-based fluids (e.g., soup, rice water, yogurt drinks), or clean water. ORS is particularly important if the child has been treated with Plan B or C or cannot return to the clinic if symptoms worsen. 6. Teach the caregiver how to prepare and administer ORS, and provide two packets of ORS for home use. 7. Advise the caregiver to give additional fluids after each loose stool: 50–100 mL for children under 2 years and 100–200 mL for children aged 2 years or older. 8. If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes before resuming fluids, administering them more slowly. Continue extra fluids until diarrhea resolves. 9. Administer zinc supplements: 10 mg daily for children under 6 months and 20 mg daily for children 6 months or older, for 10–14 days. Show the caregiver how to dissolve zinc tablets in clean water, expressed milk, or ORS for infants, or allow older children to chew the tablet or drink it dissolved. 10. Emphasize the importance of completing the full 10–14 days of zinc supplementation. 11. Continue feeding during diarrhea episodes. Breastfeeding should be maintained as often and as long as the child desires. 12. For children with dehydration undergoing rehydration (Plan B or C), withhold other foods for 4–6 hours. 13. Hospitalized children require specialized diets to ensure a daily intake of at least 110 calories/kg. Infants under 6 months should be encouraged to exclusively breastfeed. If not breastfeeding, provide a low-lactose or lactose-free breast milk substitute using a spoon or cup, not a bottle. 14. For children aged 6 months or older, restart feeding as soon as possible, offering food six times daily to achieve at least 110 calories/kg per day. Nasogastric feeding may be necessary for children with poor appetite due to serious infections. 15. Persistent diarrhea may require dietary adjustments. Two recommended diets are available for children with severe persistent diarrhea. If the first diet fails or the child does not improve after 7 days, switch to the second diet. 16. Successful treatment is indicated by adequate food intake, weight gain, fewer diarrheal stools, and absence of fever, with weight gain being the most critical criterion. 17. Add fresh fruits and well-cooked vegetables to the diet of children responding well to treatment. After 7 days of effective dietary treatment, transition to an age-appropriate diet, including milk providing at least 110 calories/kg per day. 18. Children can return home but require regular follow-up to ensure continued weight gain and adherence to feeding advice. 19. For children with non-severe persistent diarrhea, outpatient treatment is sufficient. Provide supplementary multivitamins and minerals for 2 weeks and prevent dehydration with fluids according to Treatment Plan A. 20. ORS is effective for most children with persistent diarrhea, but some may have impaired glucose absorption, requiring IV rehydration until ORS can be tolerated without worsening diarrhea. 21. Routine antibiotic treatment for persistent diarrhea is not effective and should not be used. However, specific intestinal or non-intestinal infections should be identified and treated appropriately. 22. Examine children with persistent diarrhea for non-intestinal infections such as pneumonia, sepsis, urinary tract infections, oral thrush, and otitis media, and treat accordingly. 23. For intestinal infections, treat with oral metronidazole if stool examination reveals Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites with red blood cells, Giardia trophozoites or cysts, or if diarrhea persists for more than one month without stool examination. 24. Feeding is critical for children with persistent diarrhea. Breastfeeding should be continued, and animal milk intake should be temporarily reduced. Provide complementary foods appropriate for the child’s age. 25. For infants over 4 months who have only consumed animal milk, introduce solid foods. Offer frequent small meals, at least six times daily. 26. Follow up with the caregiver after 5 days or earlier if diarrhea worsens or other problems arise. Reassess children who have not gained weight or whose diarrhea has not improved to identify underlying causes requiring immediate attention or hospital admission. 27. Dysentery is characterized by frequent loose stools mixed with visible red blood. Most cases are caused by Shigella and require antibiotic treatment. 28. Severe complications of shigellosis include intestinal perforation, toxic megacolon, and hemolytic uremic syndrome. 29. Treat dysentery with an oral antibiotic effective against local Shigella strains for 5 days. If antibiotic sensitivity is unknown, use ciprofloxacin for 3 days. For severely ill children, administer ceftriaxone IV or IM for 3 days. 30. Provide zinc supplements as for watery diarrhea. 31. Monitor for dehydration, potassium depletion, and high fever. Prevent potassium depletion with ORS or potassium-rich foods like bananas, coconut water, or dark-green leafy vegetables. 32. Never use drugs for symptomatic relief of abdominal or rectal pain or to reduce stool frequency, as they can worsen the illness. 33. Nutritional management is essential, as dysentery adversely affects nutritional status. Encourage breastfeeding and normal food intake for children aged 6 months or older. 34. If there is no improvement after 2 full days of treatment, reassess for other conditions, stop the first antibiotic, and switch to a second-line antibiotic effective against Shigella. 35. For suspected amoebiasis, administer metronidazole for 5 days. 36. Admit children requiring hospital treatment and refer to a surgeon if necessary. 37. Supportive care includes preventing or correcting dehydration and continuing feeding. Never give drugs to reduce stool frequency or relieve abdominal pain, as they can increase illness severity.
